title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
0.1 Goals
A coding agent is a collaborator with no memory and no stake in being right. It writes plausible code quickly, and plausible is not the same as correct. So the useful question is not can it fit the model — it is what can I delegate, and how do I check it?
This is the written version of a workshop given at the University of New Mexico. It is a walkthrough, not an assignment: everything in it runs on one public repository and one real research question — did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump between 2020 and 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
See the whole loop once — clone, branch, diff, undo — on a real project.
See how an agent comes to know a project through an instruction file.
Watch one substantive question get answered, and watch us check the machine’s work.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
0.2 How this is organized
Before you start — Downloads: what to install, how to check it worked, and the zero-install paths if you would rather not install anything.
The workflow — Framing on what an agent is and where it fails silently; Setup; the git workflow that makes delegation safe; and Agents, on instruction files and the commands worth knowing.
The pipeline — the overview, then one chapter per stage: the data, the recode, the analysis, the tests, and the app and publishing. These chapters run the repository’s own scripts, so the numbers and figures in them are the ones the code actually produces.
Checking the work — Verification: reading the diff, citing the codebook, reporting n, and turning a check into a test.

title: AI as a Research Tool
text:
0.3 Running the code
The repository is public, so read access is all you need:
git clone https://github.com/crweber9874/UNM_Workshop.git
cd UNM_Workshop
Rscript R/01_recode.R
Rscript R/02_analysis.R
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'
quarto render                 # rebuild this book

About the code chunks Chapters with output execute against data/wss_2020_2024.csv, which is in the repository. Results are cached with Quarto’s freeze, so rebuilding the book does not re-run everything — but deleting _freeze/ and rendering again is the real test of reproducibility.


About the data The Western States Survey file here is pared down for teaching. Variable meanings come from the codebooks in codebooks/ — cite those, not this book, and not the agent.

2.2 Platform notes
macOS. Git ships with the Command Line Tools: run xcode-select --install in Terminal. For R, download the .pkg for your chip (Apple silicon vs. Intel) from CRAN. Homebrew is a convenient alternative for everything here (brew install git node quarto, brew install --cask r rstudio visual-studio-code).

2.6 Then what
Clone the repository and check that it runs:
git clone https://github.com/crweber9874/UNM_Workshop.git

Missing packages are the usual first error. Install what the pipeline needs:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "haven", "survey", "broom",
                   "here", "scales", "testthat", "shiny"))
The Bayesian section of the analysis chapter uses brms, which compiles Stan models and takes considerably longer to install. Add it only if you intend to run that part:
install.packages("brms")
From there, continue to Setup.

title: 3  Framing: what is “AI” here?
text:
3.1 What the tool actually is
A large language model predicts text. A coding agent wraps that model in a loop: it reads files, proposes edits, runs commands, reads the output, and tries again. Three consequences follow, and they explain everything else on this site.

title: 3  Framing: what is “AI” here?
text:
It has no memory of your project beyond what it reads this session. That is why an instruction file (Agents) matters more than clever prompting.
It optimizes for a plausible answer, not a correct one. It will invent a variable name, a function argument, or a citation with complete fluency.
It acts on your files. Which is fine — if every change is visible and reversible (Git workflow).

title: 3  Framing: what is “AI” here?
text:
3.2 Software engineering vs. research code
Agents arrived from software engineering, where they are genuinely strong. Research code is a different problem.









Software
Research code




Where the spec lives
Written down; tests encode it
A codebook, a literature, your judgment


How failure appears
Loud — it crashes or a test goes red
Silent — it runs and prints a number


Cost of a subtle error
A bug report
A published claim


Agent performance
Strong
Confidently wrong




The core asymmetry A wrong recode does not throw an error. pid7 == 8 is “not sure” in this survey, not “strong Republican” — code it as the latter and your partisanship measure is quietly wrong, every model after it is wrong, and nothing in your console will say so.

title: 3  Framing: what is “AI” here?
section: 3.3 What to delegate, and what never to trust unchecked
text:
3.3 What to delegate, and what never to trust unchecked

Delegate freely Scaffolding and boilerplate · refactoring you can read · documentation · tests · debugging an error message · “explain what this script does” · translating Stata to R · the fiddly ggplot2 call you do not want to look up.


Never accept unchecked Variable coding and reverse-coding · which cases were dropped · weights and survey design · anything that cites a number · anything that cites a source.

title: 3  Framing: what is “AI” here?
text:
3.4 Where the tools differ

Copilot is strongest at the next line: inline completion while you type, and quick questions about an open file.
Claude Code (and Codex, Cursor’s agent mode, Copilot agent mode) is strongest at the next task: “add income terciles to the recode, rerun it, and show me what changed.” It edits several files and runs commands.
A chat window with no repository access is the weakest option for this work: it cannot see your data, so it guesses your variable names.

Use the first two together. That is what we set up next.

Discussion Name one task in your own current project you would hand to an agent today, and one you would not. What distinguishes them?

title: 4  Setup
text:
4.1 Why a repository at all
GitHub hosts code, data, and documents on the web. Four reasons it matters for research:

title: 4  Setup
text:
Transparency — the work is open to inspection.
Reproducibility — others can recreate and extend your analysis.
Collaboration — several people contribute to one project without emailing files.
Version control — every change is tracked, and reverting is trivial.


And for working with agents An agent edits files in place. The repository is what makes that safe: you can see exactly what changed (git diff) and undo it (git restore). Without version control, you are letting a confident stranger type into your manuscript.

title: 4  Setup
text:
4.2 What a repository looks like
A repository is a folder with your code, data, documentation, and the complete history of changes. This one:
UNM_Workshop/
├── AGENTS.md              the brief every AI agent reads
├── CLAUDE.md              one line: @AGENTS.md
├── data/
│   ├── wss_2020_2024.csv  analysis file (read-only)
│   └── wss_clean.rds      built by R/01_recode.R
├── codebooks/             2020 & 2024 survey codebooks (PDF)
├── R/
│   ├── functions.R        pure helpers, shared and unit-tested
│   ├── 00_build_data.R    raw Stata → csv (instructor only)
│   ├── 01_recode.R        all recoding lives here
│   └── 02_analysis.R      models and figures → output/
├── app/app.R              Shiny explorer
├── tests/testthat/        test-unit-* and test-integration-*
├── slides/                workshop slides (Quarto revealjs)
└── .devcontainer/         one-click Codespace
Numbered scripts, one job each, strict order. Recodes never live in analysis scripts — that single rule is what keeps four people and an agent from quietly disagreeing about what latino means.

title: 5  Git workflow
text:
5.1 The model
Changes move left to right, one deliberate step at a time, and come back with git pull. The staging area exists so you can commit some of your changes — the finished recode, not the half-written one beside it.

title: 5  Git workflow
text:
Working directory → Staging area → Local repo → Remote (GitHub)
     (edit)            (add)        (commit)        (push)
                                         ←  (pull)  ←

title: 5  Git workflow
text:
5.2 Clone (and fork, for later)
Clone makes a copy on your computer. This is what you want today:
git clone https://github.com/crweber9874/UNM_Workshop.git
cd UNM_Workshop
Your edits stay local. You can commit, branch, and break things freely; none of it touches the original, because pushing is the only operation that would, and you can only push to repositories you have access to.
Fork makes a copy under your account, on the GitHub website. That is what you’d use to contribute to a project you cannot write to — fork, clone your fork, push, open a pull request. Worth knowing; not needed here.

Today you only clone The repository is public, so read access is all you need — nobody has to be added to anything, and nothing you do locally can affect the original. Forking is for the day you want to send work back somewhere.

title: 5  Git workflow
text:
5.3 The everyday loop
git pull                     # pick up changes to the original
git status                   # what changed?
git add R/01_recode.R        # stage specific files (avoid `git add .` blindly)
git commit -m "Recode age into generations"
git diff HEAD~1              # read what you just committed
A commit is a snapshot of your changes with a unique ID and a message. The message is for the version of you who, in four months, needs to know why age_group has four categories. Write it for that person.
Every command here works in your own clone with no write access to anything. push is the only one that needs somewhere you can write.

title: 5  Git workflow
text:
5.4 Branching in your own clone
git switch -c trying-something     # a branch costs nothing
# ...edit, add, commit...
git switch main                    # back to where you started
git branch -D trying-something     # throw the experiment away
This is the whole safety net, and it is entirely local. Let the agent loose on a branch; if the result is wrong, delete the branch.

Rules of the road Branch per task, never commit on main · small commits with clear messages · read the diff before you commit · never commit data you were not given, passwords, or .Renviron.

title: 5  Git workflow
text:
5.6 Merge conflicts
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
their version
>>>>>>> main
Keep what is right, delete the markers, then git add and git commit. You can ask the agent — “resolve the merge conflict in R/01_recode.R, keeping both recodes” — and then read its diff.

title: 5  Git workflow
text:
5.7 Undo



Situation
Command




See what you changed

Discard edits to a file
git restore file.R


Unstage
git restore --staged file.R


Fix the last commit message
git commit --amend


Undo a commit, keeping the history
git revert <hash>


Throw away a branch
git branch -D name-topic


Look at the history
git log --oneline -10




Follow along, if you like Clone the repo, make a branch, let an agent change one line of R/01_recode.R, run git diff, then git restore it. That is the loop everything else today sits inside.

title: 6  Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text: 6.1 How an agent “sees” this repo

title: 6  Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
On start, it loads instruction files: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code), AGENTS.md (Copilot, Codex, Cursor…), .github/copilot-instructions.md (Copilot).
It reads files you mention (@R/01_recode.R) or that it searches for.
It runs commands (R, git) — with your permission.


The instruction file is the project brief Layout, variable meanings, conventions, guardrails. Here CLAUDE.md contains one line — @AGENTS.md — so every tool in the room shares a single source of truth. Change the brief once and all of them follow it.

title: 6  Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
6.2 What ours says
## Project
Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump from 2020
to 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?

## Layout
- data/wss_2020_2024.csv  analysis file (read-only; never edit by hand)
- R/01_recode.R           all recoding lives here
- codebooks/              cite these when describing a variable

## Rules
- R + tidyverse, native pipe |>. Minimal comments.
- New recodes go in R/01_recode.R, not in analysis scripts.
- Always report n_obs and n_miss with any model.
- Use survey weights for population estimates; say when you don't.
- Don't push to main without the user's say-so; prefer a branch + PR.

title: 6  Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
6.3 Writing a good AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md

What the project is (one sentence) and the research question.
Where things live; which files are read-only.
Variable definitions and where to cite them (codebook).
Conventions: language, style, where recodes go.
Guardrails: report N and missingness, use weights, don’t push to main.
Keep it short; agents follow concise rules better than essays.

Personal, all-project preferences go in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

title: 6  Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
6.6 Division of labor
Copilot is strongest at the next line — completions while you type. Claude Code is strongest at the next task — “add income terciles to the recode, rerun it, and show me what changed.” Use both.

title: 6  Agents: instructions & shortcuts
text:
6.7 Spending less

/clear between unrelated tasks; long context is re-billed every turn.
Point at files (@R/02_analysis.R) rather than asking it to “look around.”
Plan mode for anything large: approve the plan, then let it execute.
A smaller model for routine edits and renames.
One well-specified request beats six vague corrections.


Then verify Agents produce plausible code, and in research code failure is silent. Read the diff, check the coding against the codebook, report n_obs and n_miss, and write a test. That is Verification.

title: 7  The pipeline
text:
7.1 The question
Did Latino voters in the Western states shift toward Trump between 2020 and 2024, and does authoritarianism condition that shift?
Western States Survey (YouGov), 2020 (n = 3,600) and 2024 (n = 4,000): Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah. Codebooks: 2020, 2024.

title: 7  The pipeline
text:
latino — the YouGov race item (Hispanic).

authoritarianism — mean of four child-rearing pairs, 0–1, 1 = authoritarian response (auth1–auth4).

trump_vote — 1 Trump, 0 Biden/Harris, NA otherwise.
Weights — weight in 2020, weight_all in 2024, combined as weight.


Cite the codebook, not the agent Every claim about a variable on this page traces to codebooks/ and the variable list in AGENTS.md. When an agent tells you what a variable means, that is a hypothesis.

7.3 Run it end to end
Rscript R/01_recode.R                       # csv  -> data/wss_clean.rds
Rscript R/02_analysis.R                     # models, figures -> output/
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'

R/00_build_data.R needs the raw Stata files, which are not distributed; the CSV it produces is in the repository.

Why the order is enforced Every number traces back through exactly one path. If the recode changes, the analysis and the app change with it, because neither keeps its own private copy of the recoding logic. Ask an agent to add a recode to 02_analysis.R and it will happily do it — this is the rule you are enforcing against your own convenience.

n_miss here is non-voters, other candidates, and the ineligible — everyone for whom a two-party vote is undefined.

The puzzle A two-point Latino shift, estimated on 786 Latino respondents in 2024, is far from the double-digit national exit-poll story. Sample? Weights? Mode? Reported versus intended vote? That is the interesting part — not reproducing a headline, but establishing what this sample can and cannot support.

Source: R/02_analysis.R run on data/wss_clean.rds. The intervals in that script use a Kish effective n, not a design-based variance — fixing that would be a reasonable first change to make.

title: 7  The pipeline
text:
7.5 Four directions this could go
Any one of these is a complete demonstration of the loop — prompt, diff, n_obs, test. We walk through one; the rest are here to run later, on this repo or your own data.


Recode — add generation, income terciles, and a strength-of-partisanship measure to R/01_recode.R. Check each against the codebook, and add a test per variable.

Analysis — Bayesian logit with brms; predicted probabilities for authoritarianism × Latino × year. Does the reported/intended distinction (vote_type) matter?

Shiny — add a state-by-year panel and a download button to app/app.R.

Skepticism — is this sample representative of Latino voters? Interrogate the weights, the mode, and the comparison with external estimates.


The loop, whichever you pick Branch → prompt the agent → read the diff → report n_obs and n_miss → write the test → commit. All of it in your own clone.

title: 7  The pipeline
text:
7.6 Starting prompts worth stealing
Read AGENTS.md and R/01_recode.R. Add an income-tercile variable built from
faminc, using survey weights. Do not touch anything else. Show me the diff.

Read codebooks/wss2024_codebook.pdf for pid7 and tell me whether
R/01_recode.R codes party3 correctly. Quote the codebook.

Refit the model in R/02_analysis.R with brms, bernoulli family, weakly
informative priors. Report n_obs and n_miss. Do not drop the weights.
Each of these is narrow, names its files, and asks for evidence. That is the whole technique.

title: 9  The recode
text:
9.1 The script
One rule governs this chapter: every derived variable is created in R/01_recode.R, and nowhere else. Analysis scripts read the result; they never recode. The rule exists because an agent asked to “add a measure” will otherwise add it wherever it is currently looking, and two months later two scripts disagree about what party3 means.
#> # Recode: data/wss_2020_2024.csv -> data/wss_clean.rds
#> library(tidyverse)
#> source("R/functions.R")
#> 
#> wss <- read_csv("data/wss_2020_2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
#> stopifnot(all(c("auth1", "auth2", "auth3", "auth4", "pid7", "age") %in% names(wss)))
#> 
#> wss <- wss |>
#>   mutate(
#>     authoritarianism = auth_scale(pick(auth1:auth4)),
#>     auth_group = bin_auth(authoritarianism),
#>     age_group  = bin_age(age),
#>     party3     = pid_to_party3(pid7),
#>     race4      = fct_lump_n(race, 3, other_level = "Other") |> fct_infreq(),
#>     latino     = factor(latino, 0:1, c("Non-Latino", "Latino")),
#>     year       = factor(year)
#>   )
#> 
#> stopifnot(all(between(wss$authoritarianism, 0, 1), na.rm = TRUE))
#> write_rds(wss, "data/wss_clean.rds")

source("R/01_recode.R")
wss <- read_rds("data/wss_clean.rds")

authoritarianism is the row mean of the four items, so it is bounded 0–1 by construction — and worth checking rather than assuming:

summary(wss$authoritarianism)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
#>  0.0000  0.0000  0.5000  0.4439  0.7500  1.0000       1


rowMeans(..., na.rm = TRUE) is a decision, not a default A respondent who answered one of four items gets a score built from that one item. That may be what you want, or it may not; either way it is an imputation rule, and it should be a deliberate choice rather than an argument an agent supplied because it suppresses NAs. A stricter version requires a minimum number of items:
auth_n = rowSums(!is.na(pick(auth1:auth4))),
authoritarianism = if_else(auth_n >= 3,
                           rowMeans(pick(auth1:auth4), na.rm = TRUE),
                           NA_real_)

title: 9  The recode
section: 9.5 Asking an agent to extend it
text:
9.5 Asking an agent to extend it
A usable prompt is narrow, names its file, and asks for evidence:
Read AGENTS.md and R/01_recode.R. Add an income-tercile variable built from
faminc, weighted by `weight`. Add it to R/01_recode.R only. Then show me
the diff and a count() of the new variable.
Then check three things before you keep it: that the cutpoints are what you’d have chosen, that faminc really runs 1–16 with no missing-data codes hiding inside that range (the codebook, not range(), settles this), and that the row count of wss_clean.rds has not changed. The next chapter uses these variables; the one after makes the checks permanent.

title: 10  The analysis
text:
10.1 Weighted two-party Trump share
Every number below rests on those 6,495 respondents. Report that pair with every model you show anyone, including yourself.
shares <- voters |>
  summarise(trump = weighted.mean(trump_vote, weight),
            n     = n(),
            n_eff = sum(weight)^2 / sum(weight^2),
            .by   = c(year, latino)) |>
  mutate(se        = sqrt(trump * (1 - trump) / n_eff),
         trump_low = trump - 1.96 * se,
         trump_upp = trump + 1.96 * se)

shares |>
  select(year, latino, trump, n, n_eff, trump_low, trump_upp) |>
  arrange(latino, year) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

The Latino shift is about two points, on 786 Latino respondents in 2024 — nothing like the double-digit national exit-poll story. Whether that is a real difference, a weighting artifact, a mode difference, or the reported-versus-intended mix is the interesting question, and this table cannot settle it alone.

title: 10  The analysis
text:
The interval is approximate, and the approximation matters n_eff is Kish’s effective sample size, which discounts for unequal weights but ignores clustering and stratification. For anything you would publish, use a design-based variance:
library(survey)
des <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~weight, data = voters)
svyby(~trump_vote, ~interaction(year, latino), des, svymean)
An agent asked for “confidence intervals on a weighted mean” will usually hand you the Kish version without mentioning the assumption. That is not a bug in the agent; it is the thing you are responsible for noticing.

grid <- expand_grid(
  latino           = levels(voters$latino),
  year             = levels(voters$year),

  mutate(p   = plogis(fit),

         upp = plogis(fit + 1.96 * se.fit))

title: 10  The analysis
text:
10.3 The Bayesian version
brms is the better tool here: priors on an interaction-heavy model, and posterior summaries you can actually interpret. It is not run in the book because compiling takes longer than the whole render.
library(brms)
fit_b <- brm(
  trump_vote | weights(weight) ~ latino * year * authoritarianism +
    age + female + college,
  family  = bernoulli(),
  prior   = c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
              prior(normal(0, 2), class = "Intercept")),
  data = voters, chains = 4, cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr", seed = 1
)
fit_b                                            # n_obs is in the output header
pp_check(fit_b)
conditional_effects(fit_b, "authoritarianism:latino")

weights() in brms is not survey weighting It treats each weight as a case replication, which gives you the point estimates but understates uncertainty for a complex design. If the weights carry a design, say so in the paper, or move to a design-based estimator. This is worth stating out loud because it is precisely the distinction an agent will flatten.

The figures this chapter draws are also written to output/ by R/02_analysis.R, which is git-ignored — the repository keeps the script, not the picture.

title: 11  The tests
text:
11.1 What testthat is
A test is how you make a verification permanent. You will check a recode once by hand; you will not check it again in six weeks when somebody — you, a collaborator, an agent — “improves” it. testthat turns the check into something that fails on its own.
R’s unit-testing package. A test file is ordinary R code that asserts rather than prints: it states what must be true and fails loudly when it is not. Files live in tests/testthat/ and are named test-*.R.
The string is the failure message, so write it as a claim.

title: 11  The tests
text:
test_that("what must be true", {
  expect_true(...)
})



Expectation
Asserts



expect_equal(x, y)
equal within numerical tolerance


expect_identical(x, y)
exactly identical


expect_true(x)
all of x is TRUE



expect_setequal(x, y)
same values, any order


expect_length(x, n)
length is n



expect_error(f())
it does fail


expect_no_warning(f())
it runs clean


skip("reason")
not applicable in this environment

title: 11  The tests
text:
11.2 Two kinds of test
The suite is split by what each test needs in order to run, because that is what determines how fast it is and how precisely it points at a failure.








Unit
Integration



Files
test-unit-*.R
test-integration-*.R


What it tests
one function
the pieces working together


Input
synthetic, written in the test
the real CSV, the built .rds, the app


Fails when
the function’s logic is wrong
the wiring is wrong


Runs in
milliseconds
seconds



A unit test for bin_age() tells you the breaks moved. An integration test on data/wss_clean.rds tells you something upstream changed. You want both: the first is precise, the second is what actually catches the agent that edited the recode and broke the app.

Unit tests need units A 200-line script has nothing to unit-test. The reason R/functions.R exists — pure helpers taking data in and returning data out, no reading, no writing — is that it makes the recode’s logic testable without the survey file at all. Extracting the functions came first; the tests came second.


11.2.1 Unit: the recode helpers

#> # UNIT. Pure recode helpers, synthetic input, no survey file touched.
#> library(tidyverse)
#> source(repo_path("R/functions.R"))
#> 
#> test_that("auth_scale averages the four items onto 0-1", {
#>   items <- tibble(a = c(0, 1, 0.5), b = c(0, 1, 0.5), c = c(0, 1, 0), d = c(0, 1, 1))
#>   expect_equal(auth_scale(items), c(0, 1, 0.5))
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("auth_scale ignores partial missingness but keeps all-missing as NA", {
#>   items <- tibble(a = c(1, NA), b = c(NA, NA), c = c(1, NA), d = c(NA, NA))
#>   expect_equal(auth_scale(items), c(1, NA_real_))
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("auth_scale rejects anything that is not four items", {
#>   expect_error(auth_scale(tibble(a = 1, b = 0, c = 1)))
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("bin_auth cuts at .25 and .75, inclusive on the low side", {
#>   expect_equal(
#>     as.character(bin_auth(c(0, .25, .26, .75, .76, 1))),
#>     c("Low", "Low", "Middle", "Middle", "High", "High")
#>   )
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("bin_age uses the documented breaks and excludes under-18", {
#>   expect_equal(
#>     as.character(bin_age(c(18, 29, 30, 44, 45, 64, 65, 92))),
#>     c("18-29", "18-29", "30-44", "30-44", "45-64", "45-64", "65+", "65+")
#>   )
#>   expect_true(is.na(bin_age(17)))
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("pid_to_party3 follows the codebook's 1-7 scale", {
#>   expect_equal(
#>     pid_to_party3(1:7),
#>     c("Democrat", "Democrat", "Democrat", "Independent",
#>       "Republican", "Republican", "Republican")
#>   )
#>   expect_true(is.na(pid_to_party3(NA_real_)))
#> })

Every input here is written out in the test. Nothing on disk can make these pass or fail, so when one goes red the fault is in the function and nowhere else.

11.2.2 Unit: the estimator

#> # UNIT. trump_share() against a toy frame whose answer is known by hand.
#> library(tidyverse)
#> source(repo_path("R/functions.R"))
#> 
#> toy <- tibble(
#>   year       = factor(c(2020, 2020, 2020, 2024, 2024)),
#>   latino     = factor(c("Latino", "Latino", "Non-Latino", "Latino", "Latino")),
#>   trump_vote = c(1, 0, 1, 1, NA),
#>   weight     = c(3, 1, 1, 1, 1)
#> )
#> 
#> test_that("unweighted share is the plain mean of observed votes", {
#>   out <- trump_share(toy, "latino", weighted = FALSE) |> filter(year == "2020", latino == "Latino")
#>   expect_equal(out$trump, 0.5)
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("weights shift the share as specified", {
#>   out <- trump_share(toy, "latino", weighted = TRUE) |> filter(year == "2020", latino == "Latino")
#>   expect_equal(out$trump, 0.75)
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("n_obs and n_miss are reported and sum to the cell size", {
#>   out <- trump_share(toy, "latino") |> filter(year == "2024", latino == "Latino")
#>   expect_equal(out$n_obs, 1L)
#>   expect_equal(out$n_miss, 1L)
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("rows missing the grouping variable are dropped, not silently pooled", {
#>   with_na <- toy |> mutate(latino = factor(c(NA, "Latino", "Non-Latino", "Latino", "Latino")))
#>   expect_false(any(is.na(trump_share(with_na, "latino")$latino)))
#> })
#> 
#> test_that("an unknown grouping column fails loudly", {
#>   expect_error(trump_share(toy, "not_a_column"))
#> })

A five-row frame whose weighted mean you can do in your head is worth more than a thousand real rows whose answer you would have to trust.

#> 
#> test_that("narrowing the state filter never grows the sample", {
#>   testServer(app_dir, {
#>     session$setInputs(state = c("AZ", "CO", "NV", "NM", "UT"), by = "auth_group", wt = TRUE)
#>     all_states <- sum(est()$n_obs)
#>     session$setInputs(state = "AZ")
#>     expect_lte(sum(est()$n_obs), all_states)
#>   })
#> })

shiny::testServer() runs the server function without a browser: set inputs, read the reactives. It caught a real bug while this chapter was being written — the server was declared function(input, output), and testServer() requires session as well.

title: 11  The tests
11  The tests
text:
11.4 What a failure looks like
Change a recode and the claim goes red. Here the assertion is deliberately wrong:

library(testthat)
wss <- readRDS("data/wss_clean.rds")

test_that("trump_vote is coded for every respondent", {
  expect_equal(sum(!is.na(wss$trump_vote)), nrow(wss))
})
#> ── Failure: trump_vote is coded for every respondent ───────────────────────────
#> Expected `sum(!is.na(wss$trump_vote))` to equal `nrow(wss)`.
#> Differences:
#> 1/1 mismatches
#> [1] 6495 - 7600 == -1105
#> Error:
#> ! Test failed with 1 failure and 0 successes.

That is the useful output: the claim, the expected value, the actual value. A silent recode error produces a number; a test produces this.

title: 11  The tests
text:
11.5 Tests worth adding

One per derived variable, asserting range and allowed values.
One asserting nrow() after the recode — the cheapest guard against a join that multiplied rows.
One asserting the analysis N, so a change in missingness cannot pass unnoticed.

expect_error() on the input guard: if someone hands the recode a file without auth1:auth4, it should fail rather than produce NaN.


A good use of an agent “Read R/01_recode.R and write a testthat test for every derived variable: range, allowed values, and row count. Do not change the recode.”
Then read the tests. They are far easier to check than the recode they protect, and reading them is how you find out whether the agent understood the codebook or guessed.

title: 12  The app, and publishing
text:
12.1 Anatomy of a Shiny app
Two stages are left: an explorer so that people can interrogate the estimates themselves, and the command that puts this book on the web.
Every Shiny app is three objects and one idea.
The idea is reactivity. You never write “when the user clicks, recompute.” You declare what each output is, in terms of inputs, and Shiny works out what to re-run when something changes.
Three kinds of object in that chain, and the distinction is the whole framework:

title: 12  The app, and publishing
text:
Piece
What it is
In this app



ui
a nested list of HTML widgets
fluidPage(sidebarLayout(...))


server
a function of input, output, session

computes the estimates, draws the plot


shinyApp(ui, server)
wires them together and serves them
the last line of the file






input$by
the control


est()
reactive


output$plot
render





input$x — read-only, set by the browser. Touching input$state anywhere makes that code depend on it.

reactive({ ... }) — a computation that caches and re-runs only when something it read has changed. est() is called by both the plot and the table, and runs once.

render*({ ... }) — an output. It re-runs when a dependency changes and writes into output$plot.


The two mistakes agents make here Asking for a reactive’s value outside a reactive context (est() at the top level — “operation not allowed without an active reactive context”), and recomputing the same summary separately in each render* block instead of sharing one reactive(). The second one is not an error; it is just the app doing the work twice.


12.1.1 This app, line by line

#> library(shiny)
#> library(tidyverse)
#> source(here::here("R/functions.R"))
#> 
#> wss <- read_rds(here::here("data/wss_clean.rds"))
#> 
#> ui <- fluidPage(
#>   titlePanel("Western States Survey: Trump vote, 2020 vs 2024"),
#>   sidebarLayout(
#>     sidebarPanel(
#>       checkboxGroupInput("state", "State", sort(unique(wss$state)), sort(unique(wss$state))),
#>       selectInput("by", "Compare by", c("latino", "race4", "auth_group", "age_group", "party3")),
#>       checkboxInput("wt", "Use survey weights", TRUE)
#>     ),
#>     mainPanel(plotOutput("plot"), tableOutput("tab"))
#>   )
#> )
#> 
#> server <- function(input, output, session) {
#>   est <- reactive({
#>     wss |>
#>       filter(state %in% input$state) |>
#>       trump_share(input$by, weighted = input$wt)
#>   })
#>   output$plot <- renderPlot(
#>     ggplot(est(), aes(year, trump, colour = .data[[input$by]], group = .data[[input$by]])) +
#>       geom_point(size = 3) + geom_line() +
#>       scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
#>       labs(x = NULL, y = "Two-party Trump share", colour = NULL) +
#>       theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
#>   )
#>   output$tab <- renderTable(est())
#> }
#> 
#> shinyApp(ui, server)

Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("app")'
Read it top to bottom:


Load once, outside server. Code above ui runs a single time when the app starts, not per user and not per click. The data read belongs there.

source("R/functions.R"). The app calls trump_share() — the same function the analysis script calls. The app holds no analysis logic of its own, so it cannot drift away from the paper.

The UI names the inputs. inputId = "by" in the UI is input$by in the server. That string is the entire contract between the two halves.

.data[[input$by]] — the tidy-evaluation form for a column chosen at runtime. An agent will often write get(input$by) or paste strings together; both work until they don’t.

A weights toggle. Making “weighted or not” visible in the interface is honest, and it shows the audience how much the weighting is doing.

n_obs and n_miss in the table. Every point in the plot has a sample size behind it, and some of them are small.

12.1.2 Why it is testable
server is an ordinary R function, so it can be run without a browser — shiny::testServer() sets inputs and reads the reactives back. That is what the app’s integration tests do. Two habits make an app testable at all: keep the computation in a named function outside the app, and keep the server body thin enough to read.

What this app would need before anyone else used it Cell-size suppression, for one — a filtered panel can easily land on fewer than 30 respondents, and a point estimate drawn from them invites exactly the over-reading this project is about. Intervals, too; the plot shows points with no uncertainty at all.

title: 12  The app, and publishing
text:
12.2 Publishing
The site, the book, and the slides are one Quarto project:
quarto render                 # build everything into _site/
quarto preview                # live reload while writing
quarto publish gh-pages       # render, then push to the gh-pages branch
quarto publish gh-pages commits the rendered output to a gh-pages branch and leaves your source branch alone. GitHub Pages serves it at crweber9874.github.io/UNM_Workshop.

12.2.1 Freeze, and why it is committed
execute:
  freeze: auto
Chapters that run R store their results in _freeze/. A rebuild re-runs only what changed, which keeps the render fast and means the book can be rebuilt on a machine without the data. Delete _freeze/ and render again when you want to prove the whole thing still reproduces.

12.2.2 What is deliberately not committed








Not committed
Why



data/wss_clean.rds
regenerate it: Rscript R/01_recode.R


output/
figures and tables are rebuilt by R/02_analysis.R


_site/
rendered output; gh-pages holds the published copy


.Renviron, .env
secrets never belong in a repository


raw .dta files
not ours to distribute





The principle: commit the instructions for producing a thing, not the thing — unless the thing is expensive to produce and cheap to store, which is the argument for _freeze/.

title: 12  The app, and publishing
section: 12.3 The whole pipeline, one command at a time
text:
12.3 The whole pipeline, one command at a time
Rscript R/01_recode.R                              # csv  -> data/wss_clean.rds
Rscript R/02_analysis.R                            # models, figures -> output/
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'  # checks pass?
Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("app")'                  # explore
quarto render                                      # book + slides -> _site/
quarto publish gh-pages                            # publish
Six commands, one direction, no step that depends on something a person remembered to do by hand. That is the standard an agent has to be held to as well — and how you hold it there is the last chapter.

title: 13  Verification
text:
13.1 The four-step minimum
Agents produce plausible code. Verification is the part of the workflow that is yours, and it is short enough to do every single time.

title: 13  Verification
text:
Read the diff. git diff before you commit, or the diff in the pull request. If you cannot explain a change, do not merge it.
Check the coding against the codebook. Open the PDF. Confirm the response options, the missing-data codes, and the direction of the scale.
Report n_obs and n_miss. Every model, every time. If the N moved and nobody said why, cases were silently dropped.
Write the test. A check you run once is a check you will stop running.

title: 13  Verification
text:
13.2 Reporting N
voters <- wss |> filter(!is.na(trump_vote))
cat("n_obs =", nrow(voters),
    "| n_miss =", nrow(wss) - nrow(voters), "\n")

fit <- glm(trump_vote ~ latino * year, family = quasibinomial,
           weights = weight, data = voters)
cat("n_obs =", nobs(fit), "| n_miss =", nrow(voters) - nobs(fit), "\n")
The second pair matters most: listwise deletion inside a model formula is the most common way a sample shrinks without anyone noticing.

title: 13  Verification
section: 13.3 Turning a check into a test

title: 13  Verification
text:
13.4 Checking an agent’s factual claims







Claim it makes
How you check it




“pid7 runs 1–7 with 4 as independent”
The codebook, not the data’s range


“I dropped non-voters”
n_miss, and count() on the raw variable


“This uses survey weights”
Read the call. Look for weights =


“The 2024 weight is weight”
It is weight_all. See AGENTS.md


“Smith (2019) shows…”
Search for the citation. Assume it is invented




Reproducibility is the real test Delete data/wss_clean.rds and output/, then run the pipeline from the top. If the numbers come back identical, the work is reproducible. If they do not, something lives in a console somewhere instead of in a script.

title: 13  Verification
text:
13.5 What to trust

Trust code you have read and can explain.
Trust numbers that a script regenerates from raw data.
Do not trust a result that exists only in a chat transcript.
Do not trust your own memory of what you accepted ten minutes ago. That is what the commit history is for.
